Peptides for hair loss: what has evidence, what does not.

Peptide Chooser editorial team. Checked 2 Nov 2026.

Short answer

Finasteride and minoxidil are the FDA-approved options for hair loss, and neither is a peptide.12 Copper peptide serums are cosmetics with lab and follicle studies behind them, not large trials in people.34 Injectable peptides sold for hair are not approved for any use, and we found no human evidence for hair.

Why do people look for peptides for hair?

Because the approved options have limits. Finasteride is a daily pill that some people do not want to take, and minoxidil has to be used every day, for months, to keep working.2 Peptide products promise an easier answer: a serum, a shampoo or an injection.

The question is not whether a peptide sounds promising, but what has been shown in people. That is what this guide sorts out.

Which hair loss treatments are FDA approved?

Two, and neither is a peptide. Finasteride 1 mg is a daily pill on prescription.1 Minoxidil is a liquid or foam you put on the scalp, sold without a prescription.2

No peptide is FDA approved for hair loss. When a product is sold as a "hair peptide", it is either a cosmetic or a research-use product.

What does finasteride do?

Finasteride slows hair loss and regrows some hair in most men who take it. It is not for women who are or may become pregnant.1 Generic finasteride starts at about $10 a month with a pharmacy coupon.5

It works while you take it. Your prescriber will go through side effects with you; MedlinePlus lists them in plain words.1

What does minoxidil do?

Minoxidil helps hair grow and slows balding. It works best in people under 40 whose hair loss is recent, and it does not help a receding hairline.2

It takes at least four months, and sometimes up to a year, before you see an effect, and most new hair is lost within a few months after you stop.2

Do copper peptides (GHK-Cu) grow hair?

GHK-Cu is a small copper peptide found in serums and shampoos. The evidence for hair comes from lab work: a 2007 study tested it on human hair follicles kept alive in a dish.3 That is not the same as a trial in people, and we found no large trial in people.

Copper peptide serums are sold as cosmetics. Cosmetics do not need FDA approval, and nobody has to show that they work.4 A scalp serum with copper peptides costs about $48 (Divi Scalp Serum, one-time price).6

What about peptide shampoos and creams?

Many shampoos, conditioners and scalp tonics list peptides, such as copper peptides, among their ingredients. They are cosmetics too, under the same rules as serums.4 A peptide on the ingredient list tells you what is in the bottle, not what it does.

What about injectable peptides sold for hair?

Research-use shops sell vials of BPC-157, TB-500 and injectable GHK-Cu, and some of them market these for hair. None is approved for any use.7 In July 2026 the FDA proposed not to let pharmacies use BPC-157 or TB-500 to make medicines.8

We found no studies in people that show these injections grow hair. We list their prices and checks on our hair page and never link to the shops.

How do you tell evidence from marketing?

  • Ask which study: in people, in animals or in a dish. Only studies in people tell you about your hair.
  • "Contains peptides" on a shampoo is an ingredient list, not a result.
  • Before and after photos, a famous name and "doctor formulated" are marketing.
  • An FDA-approved product says so on its label, and its maker had to show results in people to get there.9

None of this is medical advice. A doctor or dermatologist can tell you which option fits your hair loss.
